Which States Have Daily Overtime? The Five States That Pay by the Day — and What Each One Is Worth

Direct AnswerFive states pay daily overtime in 2026 — California, Alaska, Nevada, Colorado, and Oregon. The same 4×12-hour week pays $1,400 in California, $1,300 in Texas.

Gross pay estimates

Quick Answer

Five states pay daily overtime in 2026: California, Alaska, Nevada, Colorado, and Oregon, and only Oregon's is limited to one industry. The same worker at $25 an hour on four 12-hour days earns $1,400 a week in California and Alaska, but $1,300 a week in Texas, Colorado, Nevada (at $25 an hour), and Oregon manufacturing. That is a $5,200-a-year gap for the identical schedule. Federal law counts only the week, so a daily premium only pays when the day's overtime hours are more than the week's.

The Short Answer: 5 States, and One Schedule That Proves It

Daily overtime exists in exactly five states in 2026. California pays 1.5× after 8 hours in a day and 2× after 12. Alaska pays 1.5× after 8 hours in a day. Nevada pays 1.5× after 8 hours in a 24-hour period, but only to workers earning under $18 an hour. Colorado pays 1.5× after 12 hours in a workday or 12 consecutive hours. Oregon pays 1.5× after 10 hours in a day, but only to manufacturing workers. Everywhere else, the federal rule is the whole rule. Time and a half after 40 hours in a week, and nothing for a long day inside a short week.

The five-state list is short, but the money in it is not. Take one worker at $25 an hour on the same schedule, four 12-hour days, 48 hours a week, 52 weeks a year, and run it through each rule. California and Alaska pay $1,400 a week, $72,800 a year. Texas, Colorado, Nevada at $25 an hour, and Oregon manufacturing all pay $1,300 a week, $67,600 a year. The schedule is identical, the hours are identical, and the gap is $100 a week, $5,200 a year, decided entirely by which side of a state line the work happens on. This guide prices that gap for every schedule that matters, including the ones where the daily rule pays nothing at all. Our double-time guide covers California's 2× tier in depth, and our overtime rules by state page maps all 50 states.

What Daily Overtime Actually Means

Daily overtime is a premium that fires on a single day's hours, not the week's total. The federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) has no daily rule. It requires time and a half only for hours past 40 in a workweek, and it never requires double time or a holiday premium. A state daily-overtime law adds a second trigger on top of that weekly one, and the two triggers interact in a specific way that decides whether the premium pays anything at all.

The formula for one day is simple. Hours up to the threshold are straight time, and hours past it are 1.5× (or 2× in California past 12 hours). Then the week is reconciled, and the reconciliation has one hard rule: no pyramiding. An hour is paid once, at the highest rate that applies to it. Hours already paid at 1.5× as daily overtime are not counted again toward the 40-hour weekly threshold, and daily and weekly premiums never stack on the same hour. That is why the same 10-hour day can be worth a premium in one schedule and nothing in another. The daily premium only adds money when the day's overtime hours are more than the week's overtime hours. The worked examples below show both cases, with the exact dollars.

Three things decide your answer: your state (and, in Oregon, your industry), your hourly rate (which matters in Nevada), and your schedule, meaning hours per day and days per week. Exempt salaried workers are generally not covered by overtime rules at all, daily or weekly, so this guide is for non-exempt hourly workers. If you are not sure which side of that line you fall on, our exempt vs non-exempt guide explains the test.

The Five States: Every Daily Overtime Rule in One Table

Here is every daily overtime rule in the country, with the trigger, the rate, who it covers, and the exception that most often removes it:

StateDaily triggerRateWho it coversMain exception
CaliforniaOver 8 hours a day; 2× over 121.5× / 2×All non-exempt workersAlternative workweek voted by two-thirds; farm, healthcare, and live-in domestic workers have modified rules
AlaskaOver 8 hours a day (or over 40 a week)1.5×All non-exempt workersEmployers with fewer than 4 employees; approved voluntary flexible work-hour plans
NevadaOver 8 hours in a 24-hour period1.5×Only workers earning under 1.5× the state minimum wage — under $18 an hour in 2026Written agreement for a 4/10 schedule removes the daily trigger
ColoradoOver 12 hours in a workday, or over 12 consecutive hours1.5×Non-exempt workers under the COMPS OrderWhichever calculation — daily, consecutive, or weekly — pays most; no pyramiding
OregonOver 10 hours a day1.5×Manufacturing workers only (mills, factories, canneries)Greater of daily or weekly overtime, not both; weekly hour caps in manufacturing
Federal rule (45 states)None — over 40 hours a week only1.5×All non-exempt workersA contract or union agreement can add a daily premium

Two footnotes belong on the table. First, Kentucky is not a daily-overtime state, but it pays a premium on the seventh consecutive day in a workweek, 1.5× for work on that day, which behaves like a daily rule for seven-day stretches and is priced in the seventh-day section below. Second, Puerto Rico has its own daily overtime (1.5× after 8 hours) plus double time for work on statutory rest days. And one rule applies everywhere: if you work remotely, the overtime law of the state where you physically sit and do the work generally controls, not the state where your employer is based.

Same Schedule, Five Paychecks: The 4×12-Hour Week

The anchor schedule for this guide is a worker at $25 an hour, four 12-hour days a week, 48 hours total, 52 weeks a year. Here is what each rule pays for exactly the same week:

State / ruleStraight hoursOvertime hoursWeekly grossAnnual grossvs federal rule
Federal rule (e.g. Texas)408$1,300.00$67,600.00—
California3216$1,400.00$72,800.00+$5,200.00
Alaska3216$1,400.00$72,800.00+$5,200.00
Oregon (manufacturing)408$1,300.00$67,600.00$0
Colorado408$1,300.00$67,600.00$0
Nevada (at $25 an hour)408$1,300.00$67,600.00$0

California's $1,400, step by step at $25 an hour. The overtime rate is $37.50:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Straight time in one day8 hours × $25.00$200.00
Step 2 — Daily overtime in one day4 hours × $37.50$150.00
Step 3 — One 12-hour day, total$200.00 + $150.00$350.00
Step 4 — Four days, weekly gross$350.00 × 4$1,400.00
Step 5 — Premium over the federal rule$1,400.00 − $1,300.00$100.00 a week, $5,200.00 a year

Why do Oregon, Colorado, and Nevada pay nothing extra on this schedule? Oregon manufacturing counts 2 overtime hours a day (past 10), which is 8 overtime hours for the week, exactly the same 8 the weekly rule already pays, so the daily rule adds zero. Colorado's trigger is 12 hours, and a 12-hour day is not over 12. Nevada's daily rule switches off at $18 an hour, and this worker earns $25. Only California and Alaska fire on this schedule, because their 8-hour trigger creates 16 overtime hours where the weekly rule only creates 8, and the worker is paid the greater count, 16, not 8 plus 16. One honest note: the $5,200 is a premium on this schedule, not a raise. If the schedule drops to three days, the premium changes, and if it drops to five 10-hour days, it disappears entirely, as the next section shows.

Why 10-Hour Days, 5 Days a Week, Pay the Same Everywhere

Here is the most surprising result in this guide. Stretch the same 50 hours into five 10-hour days, and every state pays exactly the same. At $25 an hour, 10 hours a day for 5 days is 40 straight hours plus 10 overtime hours, and the daily rule and the weekly rule produce the same 10 overtime hours:

State / ruleDaily OT hoursWeekly OT hoursOT hours paidWeekly grossAnnual gross
California10 (2 a day × 5)1010$1,375.00$71,500.00
Alaska101010$1,375.00$71,500.00
Oregon (manufacturing)0 (10 is not over 10)1010$1,375.00$71,500.00
Colorado01010$1,375.00$71,500.00
Nevada (at $25 an hour)01010$1,375.00$71,500.00
Federal rule (e.g. Texas)—1010$1,375.00$71,500.00

This is the no-pyramiding rule doing its work. California's daily rule does fire, two overtime hours a day, but those 10 hours are the same 10 hours the weekly rule already pays, so the employer pays them once, not twice. A worker who assumes daily overtime means "daily plus weekly" would expect $1,750 a week. The real figure is $1,375. The practical test is one subtraction: daily overtime only adds money when the day's overtime hours exceed the week's overtime hours. That happens on short weeks with long days, which is the next section. It is also why the 4×12 schedule in the previous section pays a premium while the 5×10 schedule does not, even though both are 48 and 50 hours respectively.

The 3×12-Hour Week: Where Oregon Joins In

Shorten the week to three 12-hour days, 36 hours total, under the 40-hour weekly threshold, and the daily rules finally separate from the federal rule. There is no weekly overtime at all on this schedule, so every daily overtime hour is new money:

State / ruleStraight hoursOvertime hoursWeekly grossAnnual grossvs federal rule
Federal rule (e.g. Texas)360$900.00$46,800.00—
California2412$1,050.00$54,600.00+$7,800.00
Alaska2412$1,050.00$54,600.00+$7,800.00
Oregon (manufacturing)306$975.00$50,700.00+$3,900.00
Colorado360$900.00$46,800.00$0
Nevada (at $25 an hour)360$900.00$46,800.00$0

Oregon joins the premium states here because its 10-hour trigger creates 2 overtime hours a day, 6 for the week, where the weekly rule creates none. California and Alaska create 4 a day, 12 for the week, worth $150 a week over the federal figure. Colorado still pays nothing. A 12-hour day is not over 12 hours, and 36 hours is under 40 for the week. This is the schedule that shows what daily overtime is really for. It protects workers whose hours are packed into a few long days, the exact workers the weekly rule leaves unprotected. A part-time worker on three 12-hour shifts in California earns $7,800 a year more than the same worker in Texas, for the same 36 hours a week. Our part-time conversion guide prices the annual side of short-week schedules like this one.

Nevada's $18 Cliff: When a 1-Cent Raise Costs $3,721 a Year

Nevada's daily overtime has the strangest edge in American pay law. It switches off entirely at a wage threshold. The state minimum wage is $12.00 an hour in 2026, and the daily rule applies only to workers earning less than 1.5× that, under $18.00 an hour. Earn $18.00 or more and the daily rule vanishes, leaving only the federal weekly rule. On a four-day week of 10-hour days, that cliff is worth thousands:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — One 10-hour day at $17.998 × $17.99 + 2 × $26.99$197.89
Step 2 — Four days, weekly gross$197.89 × 4$791.56
Step 3 — Same 40 hours at straight time40 × $17.99$719.60
Step 4 — Daily overtime premium$791.56 − $719.60$71.96 a week, $3,741.92 a year
Step 5 — The same week at $18.00 an hour40 × $18.00, no daily rule$720.00 a week, $37,440.00 a year
Step 6 — What the 1-cent raise costs$791.56 − $720.00$71.56 a week, $3,721.12 a year

The worker who takes the raise from $17.99 to $18.00 loses $71.56 a week, $3,721.12 a year, because the raise crosses the threshold and the daily overtime disappears with it. The breakeven rate is $19.79 an hour. Only at $19.79 does 40 straight hours ($791.60 a week) match what the $17.99 worker earns with daily overtime. Two practical points follow. First, if you earn just under $18 in Nevada on long days, a small raise is worth negotiating past $19.79, not to $18.00. Second, a written 4/10 agreement removes the daily trigger even below the threshold, so an employer can offer the schedule instead of the premium. Check whether you signed one before assuming the daily hours are paid. The threshold moves with the minimum wage, so verify the current figure with the Nevada Labor Commissioner before relying on $18.00.

Colorado's Midnight Rule: 13 Consecutive Hours

Colorado's daily rule has the highest threshold in the country, 12 hours, which makes it look like it almost never fires. It fires more often than it looks, because the COMPS Order counts two different clocks: 12 hours in a workday, or 12 consecutive hours of work. A shift that crosses midnight can trigger the second clock even when no calendar day passes 12 hours. Take a nurse or security guard on three overnight shifts a week, 6 p.m. to 7 a.m., 13 consecutive hours each, 39 hours for the week:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Straight time in one shift12 hours × $25.00$300.00
Step 2 — The 13th consecutive hour1 hour × $37.50$37.50
Step 3 — One 13-hour shift, total$300.00 + $37.50$337.50
Step 4 — Three shifts, weekly gross$337.50 × 3$1,012.50
Step 5 — Federal rule on the same 39 hours39 × $25.00 (under 40, no weekly OT)$975.00
Step 6 — Colorado premium$1,012.50 − $975.00$37.50 a week, $1,950.00 a year

Two details decide this one. First, the shift is 13 consecutive hours, so one hour is past 12 consecutive even though the hours split across two calendar days (6 hours before midnight, 7 after). A 12-hour overnight shift, 6 p.m. to 6 a.m., triggers nothing, because neither clock passes 12. Second, Colorado pays whichever calculation gives you the most, daily, consecutive, or weekly, and never more than one of them on the same hour. On a busier week of four 13-hour shifts (52 hours), the weekly rule would pay 12 overtime hours ($1,450) while the consecutive rule pays only 4 ($1,350), so the weekly figure governs and the midnight rule adds nothing. Check your own shifts against both clocks before assuming the premium applies.

The Seventh Day: California and Kentucky

Two states pay a premium for the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek, and it behaves like a daily rule. It fires on the day, regardless of the week's total. California pays 1.5× for the first 8 hours of the seventh day and 2× beyond it. Kentucky pays 1.5× for work on the seventh consecutive day. The premium matters most on short-shift weeks, because on long weeks the weekly overtime usually covers the same hours anyway.

Take seven straight days of 5-hour shifts, 35 hours for the week, under the 40-hour threshold, so the federal rule pays nothing extra:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Days 1–6, straight time6 days × 5 hours × $25.00$750.00
Step 2 — Day 7, seventh-day premium5 hours × $37.50$187.50
Step 3 — Weekly gross (CA or KY)$750.00 + $187.50$937.50
Step 4 — Federal rule on the same 35 hours35 × $25.00$875.00
Step 5 — Seventh-day premium$937.50 − $875.00$62.50 a week, $3,250.00 a year

Now run the same seven days at 8 hours, 56 hours for the week. California pays $1,600: 40 straight hours ($1,000) plus 16 overtime hours ($600), where the 8 seventh-day hours and the 8 weekly overtime hours are the same premium hours counted once. The federal rule also pays $1,600 on 56 hours. The seventh-day rule adds nothing on a 56-hour week, because the weekly rule already pays those hours. It is the same no-pyramiding logic as the 10-hour-day case. The rule is worth real money only when the week stays short: seven short days, not seven long ones. If your schedule is seven days a week, check your pay stub for the seventh-day line. Our pay-stub guide shows where premium lines appear.

The Escape Valves: 4/10 Schedules and Other Exceptions

Every daily-overtime state gives employers a legal way around the daily trigger, and workers should know which one applies to them. A signed agreement can quietly remove a premium the table above promises:

StateThe escape valveWhat it takesLimitation
CaliforniaAlternative workweek scheduleTwo-thirds of affected workers vote for it by secret ballotUp to 10 hours a day straight; past 10 is still 1.5×, past 12 is still 2×
Nevada4/10 schedule agreementMutual written agreement between employer and employeeOnly removes the daily trigger for the two extra hours a day
AlaskaVoluntary flexible work-hour planApproved plan the employee voluntarily joinsMust be genuinely voluntary — an imposed schedule does not qualify
ColoradoNone needed — the threshold is 12Standard 10- and 12-hour days never trigger itOnly the 12-consecutive-hours clock can surprise an employer
OregonGreater-of ruleEmployer pays the larger of daily or weekly overtimeManufacturing weekly hour caps still apply

Three more exceptions are easy to miss. California has modified daily rules for agricultural workers, healthcare employees, and live-in domestic workers, so the 8-hour trigger in the table is not universal inside the state. Alaska's daily rule does not apply at all to employers with fewer than four employees. And in all five states, a union contract or a written employer policy can pay more than the law requires. Several large employers pay daily overtime nationwide by policy even where no state requires it, which is worth checking before assuming your long day is unpaid. The reverse is also true: no employer policy can pay less than the state rule where one applies.

After Tax: What the California Premium Is Really Worth

The $5,200-a-year California premium on the 4×12-hour week is gross pay. Here is what survives federal tax and FICA, for a single filer in 2026 taking the $16,100 standard deduction and no state tax:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — California gross (4×12h)$1,400.00 × 52$72,800.00
Step 2 — Taxable income$72,800.00 − $16,100.00$56,700.00
Step 3 — Federal income tax$1,240.00 + $4,560.00 + 22% × $6,300.00$7,186.00
Step 4 — FICA (7.65%)$72,800.00 × 7.65%$5,569.20
Step 5 — Take-home pay$72,800.00 − $7,186.00 − $5,569.20$60,044.80 ($5,003.73 a month)
Step 6 — Federal-rule take-home ($67,600)$67,600.00 − $6,042.00 − $5,171.40$56,386.60
Step 7 — Premium actually kept$60,044.80 − $56,386.60$3,658.20 a year (70.35% of $5,200)

The premium keeps 70.35 cents on the dollar because the marginal rate on it is 22% federal plus 7.65% FICA, 29.65% in total. That is the same marginal rate that applies to any extra dollars at this income, which is why the after-tax value of the premium is smaller than the gross figure but still large: $304.85 a month, $140.70 a biweekly check. Here is the cross-check. $60,044.80 is exactly the take-home our $25-an-hour guide's sibling article computes for a $72,800 gross. Same income, same brackets, same answer, which is how you know the math is consistent. State tax would reduce both figures further. California's own rates are not included here, and neither is the additional 0.9% Medicare tax, which starts at $200,000 in wages. Our FICA guide explains the 7.65% layer, and our bonus-tax guide shows how the same marginal rate prices a one-off payment.

How to Use the Calculator

Price your own daily overtime in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Pick your state's rule in the overtime calculator: weekly-only for the 45 federal-rule states, or the CA-style daily mode for California and Alaska. And check the state page for Nevada's wage threshold, Colorado's 12-hour clock, and Oregon's manufacturing limit.
  2. Step 2 — Enter your rate, hours per day, and days per week exactly as your schedule runs. Include any overnight shift that crosses midnight.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the daily and weekly results and take the larger overtime count, never the sum. That is the no-pyramiding rule, and it is the most common error in hand calculations.
  4. Step 4 — Check the exceptions before budgeting. A voted alternative workweek, a signed 4/10 agreement, or a voluntary flex plan can remove the daily premium, and the calculator cannot see those.

Limitations

  1. Federal only unless stated: the after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. State and local taxes are left out, so actual take-home is lower in most states, including California, whose rates are not included in the $60,044.80 figure.
  2. Exempt workers are not covered: salaried exempt employees generally earn no overtime at all, daily or weekly, so this guide is for non-exempt hourly workers.
  3. State rules change: thresholds move with minimum wages (Nevada's $18.00 line is tied to the $12.00 minimum wage) and orders are revised. Verify the current rule with your state labor department before relying on it for a dispute.
  4. Industry exceptions exist: California's farm, healthcare, and live-in domestic workers have modified daily rules, and Oregon's daily rule covers manufacturing only. Your industry can change the answer.
  5. Agreements can remove the premium: a voted alternative workweek, a written 4/10 agreement, or a voluntary flexible work-hour plan can lawfully remove daily overtime. Check what you signed.
  6. Not tax or legal advice: the take-home sketches use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. Credits, other income, filing status, and multiple jobs can change your real return, and a wage claim should go through your state labor department.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about daily overtime:

Which states have daily overtime in 2026?

Five states. California pays 1.5× after 8 hours a day and 2× after 12. Alaska pays 1.5× after 8 hours a day. Nevada pays 1.5× after 8 hours in a 24-hour period, but only for workers earning under $18 an hour in 2026. Colorado pays 1.5× after 12 hours in a workday or 12 consecutive hours. Oregon pays 1.5× after 10 hours a day, manufacturing workers only. The other 45 states use the federal rule only: time and a half after 40 hours in a week, with no daily trigger at all.

Do I get overtime for a 10-hour day if my week is under 40 hours?

It depends entirely on your state. In California and Alaska, yes. Two hours of that day are paid at time and a half even if the week stays under 40 hours, because the daily rule fires first. In Oregon manufacturing, no. The trigger is over 10 hours, so a 10-hour day exactly is all straight time. In Colorado, Nevada (at $18 an hour or more), and the 45 federal-rule states, also no. Only the 40-hour weekly threshold counts, so a 10-hour day inside a short week is paid straight.

How much is daily overtime in California?

In California, hours 9 through 12 in a workday are paid at 1.5× your regular rate, and hours past 12 are paid at 2×. On the seventh consecutive day in a workweek, the first 8 hours are 1.5× and anything beyond is 2×. At $25 an hour, a 12-hour day pays $350: 8 hours at $25 ($200) plus 4 hours at $37.50 ($150). A 14-hour day pays $440: the same $350 plus 2 hours at $50 ($100). Our double-time guide works out the full day.

Does Nevada pay daily overtime?

Only for lower-wage workers. Nevada pays time and a half for hours past 8 in a 24-hour period, but only if you earn less than 1.5× the state minimum wage. That is under $18 an hour in 2026, since the minimum wage is $12.00. At $18 an hour or more, Nevada uses the federal weekly rule only. A written agreement for a 4/10 schedule (four 10-hour days) removes the daily trigger even for workers under the threshold.

Does Colorado pay daily overtime after 8 hours?

No. Colorado pays time and a half only after 12 hours in a workday, after 12 consecutive hours, or after 40 hours in a week, whichever calculation gives you the most, under the COMPS Order. An 8-hour or 10-hour day earns no premium in Colorado unless the week passes 40 hours. The 12-consecutive-hours rule is the one people miss. A 13-hour overnight shift earns one hour at 1.5× even though no calendar day passes 12 hours.

Can my employer schedule four 10-hour days without paying overtime?

In the 45 federal-rule states, yes. 40 hours a week at straight time is all the law requires, so a 4/10 schedule costs your employer nothing extra. In California, no, unless two-thirds of the affected workers vote in an alternative workweek schedule. In Nevada, a written 4/10 agreement does it. In Alaska, a voluntary flexible work-hour plan does it. And even where the schedule itself is free, the hours are not. A 4/10 week that runs long still earns weekly overtime past 40 hours.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • Only five states pay daily overtime in 2026: California, Alaska, Nevada, Colorado, and Oregon (manufacturing only). The other 45 states use the federal 40-hour weekly rule only.
  • The same 4×12-hour week at $25 an hour pays $1,400 in California and Alaska, $1,300 everywhere else. That is a $5,200-a-year gap for the identical schedule, worth $3,658.20 after federal tax and FICA.
  • Daily overtime only adds money when the day's overtime hours exceed the week's. Five 10-hour days pay $1,375 a week in every state, because the 10 daily overtime hours are the same 10 the weekly rule already pays.
  • The 3×12-hour week is where Oregon joins in. $975 a week in Oregon manufacturing vs $900 under the federal rule, while California and Alaska pay $1,050.
  • Nevada's $18 cliff is real. A raise from $17.99 to $18.00 on four 10-hour days costs $71.56 a week, $3,721.12 a year, because the daily rule switches off. The breakeven rate is $19.79 an hour.
  • Colorado counts consecutive hours, not just calendar days. A 13-hour overnight shift earns one hour at 1.5× ($1,950 a year on three shifts a week), while a 12-hour overnight shift earns nothing.
  • The seventh-day premium only pays on short weeks. Seven 5-hour days earn $62.50 a week extra in California and Kentucky, but seven 8-hour days pay the same $1,600 as the federal rule.
  • Check what you signed. A voted alternative workweek, a written 4/10 agreement, or a voluntary flex plan can lawfully remove the daily premium before it ever reaches your check.

Sources & Method

State rules: California Labor Code §510 (1.5× after 8 hours, 2× after 12, seventh-day premium; alternative workweek by two-thirds vote); Alaska Wage and Hour Act, AS 23.10.060 (1.5× after 8 hours a day or 40 a week; employers with fewer than 4 employees exempt); Nevada Revised Statutes 608.018 (1.5× after 8 hours in a 24-hour period for workers earning under 1.5× the state minimum wage, $12.00 an hour in 2026, so under $18.00, with a written 4/10 agreement exception); Colorado COMPS Order #39 (1.5× after 12 hours in a workday, 12 consecutive hours, or 40 hours a week, whichever pays most); Oregon Revised Statutes 653.261 (1.5× after 10 hours a day in manufacturing; greater of daily or weekly, not both); Kentucky Revised Statutes 337.050 (1.5× on the seventh consecutive day); federal FLSA, 29 U.S.C. §207 (weekly 40-hour rule only). After-tax figures use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. The standard deduction is $16,100, and the brackets run 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, and 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32. FICA is 7.65%: Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%. The $60,044.80 take-home on a $72,800 gross cross-checks exactly against the site's $72,800 guide. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Only five states pay daily overtime: California, Alaska, Nevada, Colorado, and Oregon manufacturing. The same 4×12-hour week at $25 an hour is worth $1,400 in California and Alaska but $1,300 in the other 45 states.
  2. Daily overtime only adds money when the day's overtime hours exceed the week's. Five 10-hour days pay the same $1,375 everywhere, because the daily and weekly rules pay the same 10 hours once.
  3. Watch the edges. Nevada's $18 cliff can make a 1-cent raise cost $3,721 a year, Colorado's 12-consecutive-hours rule catches overnight shifts, and a signed 4/10 agreement can remove the premium entirely.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
